explanation: After deleting a key, a node may fall below its minimum occupancy. First inspect a sibling. If the sibling has more than the minimum, redistribute one entry through the parent and update the separating key.

explanation: Modern servers combine very large memory capacities with complicated access characteristics. At the system level, a database that fits in memory no longer needs to organize every operation around avoiding disk I/O. That permits new engines, algorithms, and data structures, but it also invalidates assumptions inherited from disk-oriented systems. The core lesson is architectural: hardware trends justify redesign, not merely parameter tuning.

explanation: Physical layout determines which bytes are fetched together. A row store keeps the attributes of one tuple adjacent, which is helpful when a transaction reads or updates most of that tuple. A column store keeps one attribute from many tuples adjacent, which is helpful when an analytical query reads a few columns from many rows.

Main memory does not eliminate layout costs because CPUs move data through cache lines and memory channels. Loading unused attributes wastes bandwidth and cache capacity, while reconstructing a wide tuple from many columns costs work. The correct layout follows the dominant access pattern, and hybrid designs can split the difference.
key_points: Row layout optimizes tuple-oriented access.
Column layout optimizes attribute-oriented scans.

explanation: The five animation states show one mechanism. The OLTP process owns the current database pages. A fork creates an OLAP snapshot that initially shares those pages. Analytical reads therefore see a stable logical image without copying the entire database at snapshot creation time.

explanation: A radix tree descends according to chunks of the key. It needs no rebalancing, insertion order does not change the logical tree, and keys are represented implicitly by the path. The height depends on key length, not relation cardinality.
